paragraphs.t: The central idea of the chapter
— blue and underlined, in the text itself.
— plum with a dotted line; its meaning is in “Words to know”.
💬 In plain words   🧭 The chapter as a map   📖 Words to know   🔁 Read it again
Cloud architecture, cloud native, and microservices are three separate decisions; the cloud did not invent the service boundary — it made the boundary affordable.

Three different questions get mixed together under the word ‘cloud’. Where does the software run (cloud architecture)? Is it built to use an elastic platform (cloud native)? How is the application divided into services (microservices)? You can answer yes to any one without the others: a monolith can run in the cloud; a microservice suite can run in your own basement. The cloud’s real contribution is that it made many small deployable units affordable.

The CNCF: home of Kubernetes and the cloud-native toolchain, and author of the cloud-native definition.

blocks.caption: The chapter as a map: its sections and what each one holds.

runs.t: A microservice system can run in a public cloud, a private cloud, or on a cluster in a company’s own data center. A cloud account can run a monolith, a three-tier application, or a single function with no service boundaries at all.
The relationship is real, and it is a relationship between two decisions.
Cloud architecture

decides where the software runs, how failure is contained across machines and sites, and which platform services the teams may use. Microservice architecture decides how the application is divided, who owns the data, and how a business action crosses those divisions.
Cloud native is the name for the overlap, where the application is built so that it can use the cloud’s elasticity, and where microservices are one of the forms that application takes.

blocks.alt: Three layers, three questions. A yes on one does not imply a yes on the others.
blocks.caption: Three layers, three questions. A yes on one does not imply a yes on the others.

rows: Layer
The question it answers
What a yes looks like
Cloud architecture
Where does this run, and what does the platform guarantee?
Accounts or subscriptions, networks, regions and availability zones, identity, and a measured pool of compute, storage, and messaging.
Cloud native
Is the workload built for that kind of environment?
Loosely coupled parts, automated change, and some combination of containers, a service mesh, microservices, immutable infrastructure, serverless, and declarative APIs.
Microservice architecture
How is this application cut?
Independently deployable services, each owning its data, collaborating by events, queries, or sagas.

runs.t: The US
National Institute of Standards and Technology
fixed the cloud half of this in September 2011. A cloud, in that definition, offers on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid
elasticity
, and measured service. Consumers draw on infrastructure, a platform, or software.
Nothing in that definition requires the consumer’s application to be a set of microservices.
Elasticity is what makes a microservice affordable to operate: one service can grow without growing its neighbors.
Pooling
is what a platform team offers to many service teams.
The
Cloud Native

Computing Foundation’s definition, version 1.1, approved on 26 February 2024, puts microservices in the other half. Cloud-native practice deploys workloads in public, private, or hybrid clouds in a programmatic and repeatable way. It is characterized by loosely coupled systems that interoperate in a manner that is secure, resilient, manageable, sustainable, and observable. The technologies it names are a combination, and the list is explicitly non-exhaustive: containers, service meshes, multi-tenancy, microservices, immutable infrastructure, serverless, and declarative APIs. Microservices are one item on that list. Serverless is another. A system can be cloud native and use only some of them.

blocks.text: Why the two grew up together

runs.t: The history chapter already has the sequence. Amazon’s service interfaces became a public cloud in 2006, when infrastructure the company had built for itself was offered as services. Netflix’s 2008 data-center failure pushed a monolith toward Amazon Web Services and toward fine-grained services. Heroku’s
Twelve-Factor App

, in 2011, wrote the contract between an application and a platform: configuration in the environment, backing services treated as attached resources, processes that are stateless and disposable, logs as event streams. Docker in 2013 and Kubernetes in 2014 made the service instance a container the platform could place, restart, and scale. The CNCF, announced with Kubernetes 1.0 in July 2015, then hosted the projects that operate that style.
The cloud did not invent the service boundary. It made the boundary payable.

Many processes, many databases, many deployable units, and many network calls are expensive on a fixed set of machines that the team must order months ahead. They are ordinary on a platform that starts a container in seconds and bills for what ran. Fowler’s microservice premium, named in 2015, is in part a cloud bill and an operations load: distribution has a cost even when the platform is elastic.

blocks.text: Moving to the cloud is a separate step from cutting services

runs.t: Industry migration language keeps the two steps apart.
Rehosting
, often called lift and shift, moves an application onto cloud machines and leaves its architecture in place.
A monolith on a virtual machine is a cloud deployment of a monolith.
Re-architecting

is the later step, in which the team decomposes the application, gives each service its own data store, and adopts the collaboration patterns. Amazon’s own prescriptive guidance on modernization treats decomposition, integration, and decentralized data as work done so the organization can draw on what the cloud offers, not as something the move itself performs. Self-contained systems and modular monoliths can also be cloud native. They use the platform and they keep a larger boundary.

blocks.text: What the platform supplies for each microservice decision

runs.t: The pattern catalog named the decisions. A cloud platform is one place those decisions are implemented. The product names below are examples from Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud. The relationship is the capability, not the brand.

blocks.text: What cloud architecture asks that DDD does not

runs.t: A bounded context does not name a region.
Cloud architecture adds placement and blast radius. An
availability zone
is a data-center-scale failure domain. A
region
is a geography, and it is often a data-residency boundary. An account or subscription is an ownership and a
blast-radius

boundary: a team can be given its own account so that its permissions and its bill stay inside it. Network policy decides which services may call which. These cuts are orthogonal to the domain cut. A single bounded context can run in three zones. Two bounded contexts can be forbidden to share a database not only by DDD, but by the network.
The
shared-responsibility

line moves with the service model. On infrastructure as a service, the provider runs the machines’ host and the customer runs the operating system and the application. On a managed Kubernetes service, the provider runs the control plane and the customer runs the workloads. On a function service, the customer supplies the code and the provider runs the instance. Richardson’s deployment patterns — per virtual machine, per container, serverless — are choices of where that line sits. The domain model can be the same in all three. The operational model is not.

Cost and operability are the dark-matter side of the cloud. A saga is easier to host when a queue and a workflow engine are an API call away. It is still a distributed operation, with partial failure and with a bill made of requests, cross-zone traffic, idle sidecars, and many small databases.
Well-architected
reviews, such as Amazon’s, treat loosely coupled services as a reliability practice and treat cost and operational excellence as separate pillars.
A design can satisfy the reliability pillar and fail the cost pillar.
That is the microservice premium showing up in the platform.
Team Topologies gives the usual split. A platform team owns the cloud
landing zone
, the cluster, the pipeline, and the
paved road

: identity, ingress, the mesh, the log stack, and the golden path for a new service. A stream-aligned team owns one service or one bounded context, its repository, its database, and its page in the on-call rotation. The platform is X-as-a-service toward the stream-aligned teams.
Data mesh
uses the same joint for analytical data: the domain owns the data product, and the platform makes publishing it cheap.
Microservices without that platform team become a crowd of snowflake deployments.
A platform without service boundaries is a cloud hosting a monolith, which is a legitimate architecture.

blocks.text: What this fixes for the AI chapter

runs.t: An AI claim has to say which layer moved.

Generating a service repository, a container file, and a database schema is help with the application cut and with the deployment unit. Choosing a region for data residency, an account boundary, a network policy, or a second failure domain is cloud architecture. Recommending a split because the platform can scale one container, or refusing a split because the operation wants one transaction, joins the two: that is Assemblage’s dark energy and dark matter, priced by the cloud. Tools that autoscale, restart, and trace are acting on the platform’s control loop. Tools that name aggregates are acting on the domain. The research should keep those effects in separate columns.

The history of AWS, Netflix, Docker, Kubernetes, and the CNCF is the history chapter of this series. Chris Richardson, deployment and collaboration patterns, microservices.io. Amazon Web Services prescriptive guidance on decomposing monoliths. Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais, Team Topologies (2019).

blocks.title: Read it again: three things to carry away

paragraphs.t: Cloud architecture, cloud native, and microservices are three decisions, not one.
The cloud made the service boundary payable; it did not invent it.
Zones, regions, accounts, and cost are cuts that domain-driven design does not name.
